author: Karen Russell
en_title: The Antidote: When the Memory Bank Fails
zh_title: 《The Antidote》：尘暴过后，镇上寄存的记忆不见了
en_deck: A prairie witch has lost the memories entrusted to her. Across a ruined Nebraska town, a thriving field and an unreliable camera make it harder to decide what has survived.
zh_deck: 一位草原女巫失去了镇民寄存的记忆。一块幸存的麦田仍在生长，相机也开始偏离时间：尘暴之后，究竟有什么被留下了？
en_notice: Introduces the premise, characters, and magical devices, leaving the murder mystery, further revelations about the characters, and the ending to the novel. Includes bereavement, abuse, harm to animals, and colonial violence.
zh_notice: 介绍故事起点、人物处境与奇幻设定，保留案件真相、进一步的身世揭示及结局。小说涉及丧亲、虐待、动物受难和殖民暴力；人名沿用英文。
en_body:
The last thing a woman who stores other people’s memories wants to feel is weightless.

She wakes in a jail cell while a dust storm overwhelms the Nebraska town of Uz. Something has changed inside her. For fifteen years she has taken deposits: things her neighbors cannot endure remembering, things they cannot bear to lose. Now the deposits are gone. Her strangely light body is the first indication that a business has failed.

This is the predicament in the [publisher’s opening extract from Karen Russell’s The Antidote](https://penguinrandomhouselibrary.com/book/?isbn=9780593802250). The woman calls herself the Antidote. She is a prairie witch, a profession in which a person can rent space inside herself to someone else. Customers leave memories with her and can later withdraw them. During the transaction she enters a trance; afterward, she knows as little about the contents as a vault knows about its valuables.

The arrangement offers a seductive compromise. You have not destroyed your past. You have put part of it somewhere safe until you feel able to carry it again.

Then Black Sunday comes. Outside the cell, farms and livelihoods are disappearing into the storm. Inside, another kind of savings has vanished. The witch will have to face people who paid for something she may no longer be able to return. A magical premise has acquired the extremely practical problem of an angry customer.

## The woman behind the promise

The opening’s bodily detail is immediately compelling. Stored memories have pressure and weight even when the Antidote cannot inspect them. After their disappearance, lightness feels frightening. The familiar burden was also how she knew herself.

Her name promises relief, but her circumstances offer little evidence of ease. She needs to make a living. Her customers must trust her, while the local sheriff can threaten her. People who depend on her services can still regard her with contempt. Her usefulness has not brought security.

That contradiction gives the premise somewhere to go beyond the cleverness of memory storage. A deposit creates a relationship, even if the point of the transaction is to stop thinking about something. There is payment, an undertaking, and the expectation of a future return. What feels like a private withdrawal from the past can become another person’s obligation.

The witch has a past of her own. In her [conversation with Jane Ciabattari for Literary Hub](https://lithub.com/karen-russell-on-what-natural-disasters-can-reveal-about-the-human-condition/), Russell describes Antonina Rossi as a mother who remains in Uz hoping that her lost son will find her. Her ability to keep other people’s memories sits beside a loss she continues to remember.

This is a more interesting figure than her grand professional name initially suggests: a woman offering a remedy while living with something it cannot remedy for her. The name is a sales pitch as well as an aspiration. Russell discusses its extravagant promise in the same interview, along with the costs of burying what people need to understand about their lives.

There is room here for a reader’s hesitation, too. Anyone who has wanted a little distance from a painful memory can understand the appeal of her trade. In [Scott Simon’s NPR interview](https://www.wlrn.org/2025-03-08/karen-russell-discusses-her-new-book-the-antidote-set-during-the-dust-bowl), Russell acknowledges that we cannot keep the whole of our past continuously present. The sharper question is what becomes unavailable along with the pain: a possibility, a responsibility, a means of understanding why life has taken this shape.

## His wheat is still growing

While the Antidote discovers that she has lost too much, Harp Oletsky discovers that he has retained an inexplicable amount. His crops survive when those of his neighbors do not. His wheat continues growing in a landscape that offers no convincing reason for growth.

In the Ciabattari interview, Russell describes the farmer’s strange good fortune as a source of fear. The idea has immediate force. A blessing can become difficult to inhabit when everyone around you is suffering. The intact field feeds Harp, but it also makes him conspicuous. Why should this patch of ground be spared?

The historical setting helps that question feel physical. Black Sunday was the great dust storm of April 14, 1935; Uz is invented. The novel places an impossible harvest inside a recognizable catastrophe, where weather and ruined soil have destroyed the ordinary connection between work and reward. You do not need to solve the mystery to imagine the unease of looking over the fence.

Harp is also learning to live with his niece, Dell, whose mother, his sister, has been murdered. The two have lost the same person without acquiring the same language for the loss. Being related gives them a household; it does not immediately tell them how to share it.

Dell has her own urgent concerns. She captains a basketball team and wants to learn the prairie witch’s craft. Basketball is a particularly welcome detail among storms, murders, and magic. It gives her teammates, ambitions, habits, and reasons to be impatient. There are still things a girl wants to accomplish this week.

The contrast between a game’s rules and grief’s disorder is one possible way to approach her determination. But the game also deserves to remain a game: something she cares about, not simply an illustration of the thing that has happened to her.

A talking scarecrow further disturbs the farm’s apparent boundaries. Even the object usually left standing in the background has a voice. Russell’s cast invites us to look around rather than settle too quickly on one person as the owner of everything the town might mean.

## A photograph of the wrong moment

Cleo Allfrey arrives with a different assignment. A Black photographer working for a New Deal government project, she has been sent to document rural poverty. Where the witch receives experiences people want removed from daily consciousness, the photographer tries to make circumstances visible to people elsewhere.

Her camera complicates the assignment. Its pictures do not reliably show the instant at which she pressed the shutter. They can reveal the past or possible futures. She has an image in front of her without necessarily knowing which world it belongs to.

In her [BOMB conversation with the composer Missy Mazzoli](https://bombmagazine.org/articles/2025/03/17/karen-russell-by-missy-mazzoli/), Russell discusses both this invention and the historical photographs incorporated into the book. Some of those real images have holes punched through their negatives. Roy Stryker, who directed the documentary project that inspired Cleo’s assignment, used a hole punch to reject pictures.

The holes make selection visible. A camera was there; somebody made an image; another person decided against its circulation. What survives in an archive is shaped by more than the moment of exposure. Russell also discusses the political pressures that favored particular kinds of subjects, including the greater usefulness of images of white farmers in attracting support.

That history gives Cleo’s work a difficulty no technical improvement can remove. She wants the people in her photographs to matter to distant viewers. The viewers may prefer a more convenient image of suffering than the lives in front of her can provide.

The magical camera opens a further gap. A field has a history before its present owner begins counting his losses. Looking at the ground through a different time can disturb the assumption that a disaster story begins with the disaster. Someone may already be absent from the picture we were taught to recognize.

This is the most intriguing connection between the two occupations. The witch’s customers deliberately set memories aside. The photographer works within arrangements that decide what will be available to remember. One exchange happens inside a body, another through images that travel. Both give the question of memory a material life.

## Room for the people, and the sentences

These premises suggest a novel for readers who enjoy an invented world pressing closely against an ordinary one. Magic has customers and working conditions. A thriving crop affects a farmer’s standing with his neighbors. A girl can be interested in witchcraft and still have a basketball team to worry about.

The public opening also offers a direct taste of Russell’s prose. The Antidote searches her body for what is missing; the atmosphere outside seems to acquire a body of its own. Weight, breath, marrow, and wind turn an abstract loss into something that can be felt. It is worth trying a few pages for the movement of the sentences before deciding how interested you are in the larger mysteries.

The abundance has possible drawbacks. In her [Chicago Review of Books review](https://chireviewofbooks.com/2025/03/11/the-antidote-karen-russell/), Malavika Praseed praises the imagination and prose while finding that some narrative threads disperse the book’s force. She also questions passages of concentrated argument that slow its later movement. That is a useful qualification for anyone expecting a single, steadily tightening mystery.

The invitation offered by the opening and these conversations is more expansive: spend time with several people whose needs do not neatly coincide, in a place where even the ground cannot be taken for granted.

The dust has changed what Uz looks like. One woman is trying to understand the empty space inside her. One farmer is trying to understand what has been left standing. A photographer is waiting to see which moment will appear in the developing image. Before asking what lesson connects them, it is worth wanting to know what each will do next.
zh_body:
在内布拉斯加州的小镇Uz，有些事情可以不必一直记在心里。只要付钱，就有人替你保存：无法再承受的痛苦，不愿对别人提起的羞耻，甚至太珍贵、舍不得在日复一日的回想中磨损的快乐。

提供这种服务的女人自称The Antidote，意思是“解药”。她是一位草原女巫，以身体为别人的记忆提供寄存处。客户将故事交给她之后，可以暂时不再想起，日后仍有机会取回。她在接收记忆时进入恍惚状态，醒来后并不知道每一桩秘密，倒像一间不知道自己保存着什么的保险库。

直到1935年的那场大尘暴。她在牢房里醒来，发现身体变得可怕地轻。为镇民保管了十五年的记忆，竟然不见了。

[Knopf／Penguin Random House的公开开篇](https://penguinrandomhouselibrary.com/book/?isbn=9780593802250)把读者带到这场危机中。镇民的农田和房屋正被风沙摧毁，她经营的另一种储蓄也突然破产。有人丢了收成，有人可能再也取不回一段往事；而一个收藏了那么多秘密的小镇，未必会温和地对待那个无法兑现承诺的人。

## 解药也有自己的生活

把记忆存进另一个人的身体，保留着一种安慰：我并没有抛弃过去，只是不想现在面对它。等以后有了力气，还可以再拿回来。许多看似难以放下的事，就这样获得了一个可以延期的安排。

然而，延期需要有人承担。女巫收钱，提供服务，也承受那些寄存物带来的身体感觉。公开试读中的叙述很有触感：记忆会以重量和压力的方式存在。因此，突然变轻对她而言并不是解脱，而是失去了判断自己状况的熟悉依据。

她的别号很响亮，实际生活却没有相称的体面。她在小镇上做生意，需要顾客信任，也要面对怀疑、侮辱和当地权力的威胁。一个人可以被频繁使用，同时仍然不被尊重。镇民既希望她承担自己的过去，又未必愿意把她当成一个拥有过去的人。

她当然也有自己的名字，Antonina Rossi，还有自己的失去与等待。在[作者接受Jane Ciabattari的访谈](https://lithub.com/karen-russell-on-what-natural-disasters-can-reveal-about-the-human-condition/)中，Russell谈到，她是一个多年等待失散儿子的母亲。这个背景使“记忆保管者”有了另一层生活：她帮助别人把往事存放起来，自己却有无法这样处理的牵挂。

她要谋生，也曾向顾客许下过于漂亮的承诺。等到记忆丢失，经济上的恐惧与对这份工作的疑问一起压上来。保险库空了，意味着有人来要求兑现时，她必须回答。那些原本被安放在私人意识之外的往事，会通过顾客、账目和承诺重新进入关系。

对一个伤心的人来说，能够暂时喘息可能已经很重要。Russell在[Scott Simon主持的NPR访谈](https://www.wlrn.org/2025-03-08/karen-russell-discusses-her-new-book-the-antidote-set-during-the-dust-bowl)中也谈到，人不可能随时携带自己全部的记忆。读者可以带着这个犹豫进入故事：哪些东西被搁置之后，连理解自己处境的机会也一起丢失了？这个问题很难只靠站在局外说一句“应该记住”来回答。

## 别人的麦田没有了，他的却还绿着

在女巫为自己的破产惊慌时，农人Harp Oletsky遇到了一件相反的怪事。他的土地竟然没有像邻居那样毁坏，庄稼还在生长。尘暴席卷整个小镇，他的农场却像处于一种无法解释的庇护中。

Russell在与Ciabattari的访谈中谈到，好运使Harp感到害怕。为什么偏偏是我？这片绿地能够使他活下去，也使他与邻居之间出现了一道越来越醒目的区别。

故事所处的时代，正是美国大萧条与Dust Bowl尘暴灾难交叠的年代。“黑色星期日”指1935年4月14日的巨大尘暴；Uz则是作者创造的小镇。空气里吞没日光的尘土有历史依据，唯一幸存的麦田却带着民间故事般的疑问。

Harp是波兰移民的后代，也是一个需要学习照顾人的舅舅。妹妹遭到谋杀后，她十几岁的女儿Dell来到他身边。两个人失去的是同一个人，却并不因此就知道该怎样向对方表达悲伤。亲属关系给了他们一起生活的理由，相互理解仍然需要另外发生。

Dell还有许多眼前的事情要管。她是篮球队长，认真对待训练和比赛，也想学习女巫的本领。篮球放在尘暴史诗里，乍看有点不搭，却恰好能使这个女孩从“失去母亲的孤儿”这一概括中走出来。她有自己的队伍、目标和脾气。

比赛可以练习，可以争取，可以知道自己有没有进球。与丧亲后的茫然相比，这份清楚的秩序也许能帮助读者理解她的执着。不过，篮球也有它本身的吸引力：一个女孩仍然想把下一场比赛打好。

在这片田地附近，还有一个会发声的稻草人。暂时不必追究它的来历，光是让一个平时站着不动的东西进入叙述，就已经改变了农场的样子。读者以为属于人的故事，又出现了另一个观察的位置。

## 摄影师来到小镇，相机却没有只拍下现在

后来来到Uz的Cleo Allfrey，是一位黑人摄影师，受政府机构委派记录乡村贫困。她的相机却不肯老实记录眼前：照片有时显出过去，有时指向可能的未来，冲印结果未必对应按下快门的时刻。照片明明留下了某种东西，她却不能立刻说明自己究竟拍到了什么。

这让她的工作与女巫形成一个有趣的对照。女巫替人把某些经历从日常意识里收起来，摄影师则要使一部分处境被别人看见。可是，看见也并不简单。拍摄哪些人，用怎样的角度呈现，什么样的照片更可能得到回应，都影响着这项工作的结果。

尤其是Cleo自己也知道种族如何影响观看。她站在镜头后面，并不意味着已经离开了那些判断。哪些面孔更容易被认为值得救助，哪些苦难更容易获得重视，是她无法只用技术解决的问题。

书中穿插了真实的历史照片，其中一些留着孔洞。Russell在[与作曲家Missy Mazzoli的BOMB访谈](https://bombmagazine.org/articles/2025/03/17/karen-russell-by-missy-mazzoli/)中，谈到被打孔作废的摄影底片，以及这些图像如何进入作品。孔洞使删减留下了可见的痕迹：有人按下过快门，也有人决定这张图像不该继续流通。

异常的相机又改变了小镇的景深。一块土地可能有现任主人不知道的生活。我们容易把灾难故事从灾难降临时算起，先认识遭受损失的人，却不一定追问，此前有哪些人曾经生活在这里，又为何不在我们所见的画面中。

女巫的寄存与摄影师的记录，让记忆有了不同的去处。一些东西被有意搁置，另一些东西可能从一开始就没有进入流传下来的图像。小说的这组设定值得跟随，也因为两个从事这些工作的人，都不能完全控制它们接下来的变化。

## 为人停留，也为句子停留

如果喜欢民间传说般的奇异设定，又愿意进入有具体历史重量的长篇，《The Antidote》很值得注意。这里的人仍然要种地、赚钱、照顾亲人，天气仍然能够让一年的劳动失去结果，只是记忆会被寄存，稻草人能够开口，照片也会偏离时间。

这些设定先把读者带到具体的麻烦面前。女巫的能力形成一门生意，也产生无法兑现的债；农场的异样改变人与邻居的关系；一个女孩想学魔法，又不能因此不在乎篮球。奇幻与日常的碰撞，已经足以使人想知道接下来会发生什么。

公开节选里的语言同样有吸引力。Russell让抽象的状态获得身体感，也让风沙中的景物变得像活物。可以先读几页，看看她怎样写重量、呼吸和失去。愿不愿意为这些句子停留，是进入这本书的另一种判断。

关于全书的丰盛，[《Chicago Review of Books》的Malavika Praseed](https://chireviewofbooks.com/2025/03/11/the-antidote-karen-russell/)提出了一点保留。她肯定想象力与文字，同时认为多个人物、多项议题分散了投入，部分集中的议论打断叙事。如果希望尽快沿一条明确的情节线找到谜底，这个提醒值得放在心上。

尘暴已经把Uz熟悉的样子吹乱了。有人发现自己保管的东西空了，有人发现自己留下的东西太多，还有人举起相机，却不再知道镜头会交还哪一个世界。先不急着归纳他们共同说明了什么，看看这些人接下来怎样面对彼此，就已经是一个很好的开始。
en_source_note: This introduction begins with Knopf’s public opening and draws on Karen Russell’s conversations with Jane Ciabattari, Scott Simon, and Missy Mazzoli. Discussion of the prose concerns that opening; the interviews supply the wider character and historical context. Malavika Praseed’s review provides an assessment of the full novel’s structure.
